statements.quote:
Through
five in-person co-design workshops with 28 participants, we identified design requirements for AI inter-
ventions in brainstorming (§4, Figure 6) and implemented a public AI tool to fulfil them:
(https://social-dynamics.net/ai-risks/interventions/).
statements.locator: PDF p. 3, section 1, contribution (2).

statements.quote:
We conducted a scoping literature review of AI tools for impact assessment following the PRISMA approach [81]
(full search strings in Appendix §A).
statements.locator: PDF p. 4, section 2.2, opening sentence.

statements.quote:
Hence, we identified 30 structured brainstorming methods with potential to
fulfil the requirements for AI impact assessment (Appendix Table 7) from three sources: (1) the Millennium Project,
a peer-reviewed collection of Strategic Foresight methods [38] used in risk assessment platforms [1, 34, 100], (2)
the United Nations Futures Lab, used in AI policy making including the Futures Wheel approach [61, 104], and (3)
the UK government, using Strategic Foresight methods for AI management [48, 100, 101].
statements.locator: PDF p. 5, section 3.1; pointer to the brainstorming-method selection table in Appendix B.

statements.quote:
We asked teams to select two AI-use stakeholders—one
relatable and one not—from a template varying in backgrounds, gender, age, and jobs (Appendix Figure 10), or
they could create their own.
statements.locator: PDF p. 6, section 3.1, Empathy Mapping; points to Appendix Figure 10.

statements.quote:
Using a string-based search for AI-assisted brainstorming in general (Appendix A.1), we identified three dimensions
along which interventions in brainstorming should be conceived (Table 1).
statements.locator: PDF p. 6, section 3.2, opening sentence; points to Appendix A.1.

statements.quote:
The team then
received a description of their AI use case: the “conversational agent, Salieri, which uses text-to-speech and language
processing to provide companionship and emotional support” (Appendix Figure 7).
statements.locator: PDF p. 7, section 4, Study setup; task materials in Appendix Figure 7.

statements.quote: We collected post-workshop feedback on structure, timing, and design requirements:
statements.locator: PDF p. 8, section 4, Data collection (describes collection, not public release).

statements.quote:
We audio-recorded and transcribed interactions during in-person sessions and conducted a two-coder
inductive thematic analysis of the discussions and responses to identify design requirements [13]. This involved
two-coders identifying themes as they emerged, taking notes during the workshops, and creating a set of coded
themes, then revising the themes based on the collected post-study qualitative written questions. Annotators
met across three rounds to compare and finalise themes. We used this qualitative approach throughout the
formative/codesign workshops.
statements.locator: PDF p. 8, section 4, Analysis (describes recordings, transcripts, notes, and coding, not public release).

statements.quote:
We developed the AI tool as a sidebar for Miro users using
the Miro API, with PHP and JavaScript connecting to the OpenAI API to provide a chat interface powered by
prompt-tuned GPT-4.1.
statements.locator: PDF p. 8, section 4, Implementation of the preliminary AI tool (software implementation description, not a source-code deposit).

statements.quote:
The
tool could place sticky notes, semantically cluster impacts, and suggest additional ones (Appendix Figure 6). We
provide all prompts in Appendix E.
statements.locator: PDF p. 8, section 4, Implementation of the preliminary AI tool; Appendix Figure 6 and Appendix E.

statements.quote: To prevent redundancy, we also fed existing Miro board content into the prompts (Appendix E).
statements.locator: PDF p. 9, section 4, Implementation of the final AI tool.

statements.quote:
We present the full information for reproducing the studies discussed in the related work using our PRISMA-
based approach (searching for tools up to July 2025). We canvassed existing AI methods used in any capacity for
generating benefits, risks and/or mitigations for AI using the following search string across ACM Digital Library,
and IEEE Xplore:
statements.locator: PDF p. 21, Appendix A, opening paragraph (literature-review search materials).

statements.quote: Beyond the description in the main text, we provide the full instructions and steps for the brainstorming methods:
statements.locator: PDF p. 22, Appendix B, opening sentence.

statements.quote:
In our study we designed a final requirements codebook based on the qualitative findings from the participants.
While we present the tool and its modules in the main paper, we also provide a breakdown of each technical
component of the tool in Table 8, which includes the full initial and final design requirements; as well as detailed
annotations for each feature in Figure 6.
statements.locator: PDF p. 23, Appendix C, opening paragraph.

statements.quote:
Full annotated breakdown of each module in our AI tool. The top left panel shows the initial design requirements
gathered in our formative workshops, and the final requirements gathered in the co-design workshops. The top right
panel shows how we built the initial requirements into the Initial AI tool. The bottom panels show how we built the final
requirements into the Final AI tool.
statements.locator: PDF p. 24, Figure 6 caption.

statements.quote: AI-generated content was marked with special symbols to clearly distinguish it from human input [44].
statements.locator: PDF p. 25, Table 8 footnote (output-origin marking, not participant identifiers).

statements.quote: For transparency, we include a breakdown of each workshops’ demographics:
statements.locator: PDF p. 26, Appendix D, opening sentence; aggregate demographics in Table 9.

statements.quote:
All prompts use GPT-4.1 [gpt-4.1-2025-04-14], except for the ‘Related AI Incidents’ feature (which uses the GPT-4o
search preview [gpt-4o-mini-search-preview-2025-03-11] for retrieving live web information). The prompts are the
versions used in the co-designed version (Final AI) of the Miro-embedded tool.
statements.locator: PDF p. 27, Appendix E, opening paragraph; prompts follow on pp. 27-31.

statements.quote:
Across each workshop, participants were assigned only one AI use for the full workshop. Participants were
instructed to imagine themselves as workers at the company of their assigned AI use. They were advised to use
creative liberties as to what role(s) they would want to see themselves at in the company when devising the list
of benefits, risks, and mitigations for the Salieri chatbot companion or ArcLight medical kidney allocation AI.
statements.locator: PDF p. 32, Appendix F, opening paragraph (AI use cards).

statements.quote: The description of the AI use for the chatbot companion workshops (Formative, and Full Study’s Workshops 1–9).
statements.locator: PDF p. 32, Figure 7 caption.

statements.quote:
The description of the AI use for the medical kidney monitoring and transplant allocation AI use workshops (Verification
study for testing the AI tool’s robustness on a high-stakes tangential embodied medical AI system, Workshops 10–12).
statements.locator: PDF p. 32, Figure 8 caption.

statements.quote:
All workshops include a short 5–10 minute demo to help familiarise participants with the brainstorming method and
Miro (with or without the AI tool). For these interactive tutorials/demos, we consider an autonomous car AI use.
statements.locator: PDF p. 32, Figure 9 caption.

statements.quote: We provide screenshots from the workshops for supplementary material/screenshots of the study below.
statements.locator: PDF p. 33, Appendix F.1, opening sentence; Figures 11-12 on p. 34.

statements.quote:
Persona selection/customisation screen for the Chatbot Companion (left) and Medical AI (right) Empathy Mapping
workshops.
statements.locator: PDF p. 33, Figure 10 caption.

statements.quote:
In the main sections, we discuss the process of expert-annotation of the workshop teams’ AI impacts (Section 5.1).
We present a screenshot of the expert-annotation screen in Figure 13.
statements.locator: PDF p. 34, Appendix G, opening paragraph; Figure 13 on p. 35.

statements.quote: Semantic similarity for AI-generated vs. human-generated benefits (left), risks (middle), and mitigations (right).
statements.locator: PDF p. 35, Figure 14 caption; aggregate distribution plot.

statements.quote:
While our study uses different brainstorming methods to control for different modes of ideation (divergent and
convergent thinking), to increase the robustness of our findings regarding our main contribution (i.e., the AI tool
for assisting team brainstorming of AI impacts), we also present supplementary findings on the effects of each
brainstorming method. We also explored the overall semantic diversity of generated impacts (Figure 14).
statements.locator: PDF p. 36, Appendix H, opening paragraph; supplementary Tables 10-11 follow.

deposits.notes: The paper links this page in contribution (2), PDF p. 3, describing a public AI tool. The page matches the paper title and describes its workshops. Its 'Code and data' section states exactly: 'Fill in the form to receive the link to the datasets:'. The form asks for Lastname, Name, Institution, Email address, and 'Reason for requesting the data (max 100 words)'. It also states: 'N.B.: If you do not receive the instruction message within a few hours, please check your junk/spam e-mail folder just in case the email was moved there.' No dataset filenames, sizes, download URLs, data dictionary, or dataset license were exposed in that section. Inspection stopped at the request form; it was not submitted, and no personal information was sent. Whether delivery is automatic or subject to manual approval is unconfirmed. The advertised datasets could not be inspected, so study coverage, row structure, participant identifiers, treatment assignment, outcomes, and idea texts remain unknown. No named repository identifier was exposed from which an OSF, Dataverse, Zenodo, Dryad, Figshare, or GitHub file-list API could be called. The article's CC BY 4.0 license is not assumed to license the uninspected datasets.

notes:
Checked 2026-10-09 with Python urllib and User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1. Read the complete 133194-character markdown conversion, including References and Appendices A-H, and checked quoted passages against the 36-page local PDF (arXiv:2604.27997v1, 30 April 2026). Quotes retain the PDF text extraction's line breaks and line-end hyphenation. The paper contains no explicit participant-data release, data-on-request, analysis-code repository, or preregistration statement. Its one study-specific external availability link describes a public AI tool. The overall on_request status is supported by the dataset-request instructions on that paper-linked project page, not by an explicit on-request sentence in the PDF; an account or manual approval requirement was not established. Data-collection and implementation quotations document what was collected or built, not proof of release. Appendix materials include instructions, prompts, task/persona cards, interface and annotation screenshots, aggregate workshop demographics, supplementary tables, and a semantic-distance figure. These do not establish a downloadable participant-level dataset or an output-to-participant mapping. The preprint located through DataCite is not counted as a separate data deposit. The form's data_and_code.data_url and code_url are empty, and final.open_items is absent (there is no final key), so there is no missing-statistics list to map. Without inspected raw data, no additional per-person means, SDs, SEs, outcome-specific analyzed counts, or participant-based text-diversity measures can be confirmed as computable. Workshop outputs are team products; individual attribution must not be assumed. The form marks assignment as not_stated for S1, S2, and S3; this check does not establish that any study was randomized.

Link checks: https://social-dynamics.net/ai-risks/interventions/ returned HTTP 200. https://doi.org/10.1145/3805689.3812299 and https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3805689.3812299 each returned HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' challenge, so publisher supplementary files could not be assessed; no attempt was made to pass the challenge. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27997 returned HTTP 200 and showed only the v1 submission, with links to PDF, HTML, and TeX source but no study-specific dataset link in the returned page. Generic arXiv code-discovery widgets are not evidence of a deposited dataset. Bibliography links to other studies or external tools/data sources, and example URLs inside prompts, are not deposits of this paper's participants.

All final repository-API searches listed in searches returned HTTP 200. Endpoints were https://api.datacite.org/dois?query=..., https://zenodo.org/api/records?q=..., https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/search?q=..., and https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/?filter[title]=.... The two initial Zenodo requests used size=100 and returned HTTP 400 because anonymous searches permit at most 25 results; both were repeated successfully with size=25, and the listed counts are the successful results. DataCite title/full-name/refined-author searches returned only preprints, including this paper. The broad DataCite surname query returned 1412 results and was not exhaustively screened; it was narrowed to creators.name:(Govers AND Jarod), which returned three preprints. Broad Zenodo Govers and Harvard Dataverse Govers queries returned 117 and 355 results respectively; their first 25 and 100 records were screened and yielded no relevant deposit, then Govers AND Jarod returned zero in both services. OSF's specified endpoint filters node titles, so the Govers query is a surname-in-title search, not an exhaustive contributor search. No matching OSF node was returned by the full title, Govers, or AI Impact Assessment queries. No relevant public deposit with inspectable participant or output rows was found. Confidence is medium because the advertised datasets were not accessible without a request, the publisher was blocked, and absence from these searches cannot establish absence of all possible public deposits.
